name: Lookups in a turned ring buffer
brief:
A ring buffer holds distinct order ids that were stored in rising order, but the read pointer has moved, so `ring` is that sorted list turned round at some point (perhaps not at all). For each id in `targets`, find the position in `ring` of the smallest id that is at least the target, or `-1` if every id is smaller.

Write `find_in_ring(ring, targets)`, which returns the positions in the order of `targets`.

Example. For `ring = [40, 50, 10, 20, 30]` and `targets = [20, 45, 55]` the id 20 sits at position 3 and 45 is met by 50 at position 1. Every id is below 55. The answer is `[3, 1, -1]`.
constraints: $0 \le n, q \le 100{,}000$; ids are distinct whole numbers between $-10^9$ and $10^9$.

$O(\log n)$ time per lookup is the target. Scanning the ring for each id is too slow, and a lookup by exact value cannot answer for an id that is absent. Stepping up from an absent id to the next present one can take up to $10^9$ steps.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: First find where the smallest id sits with one binary search against the last entry. Then search the sorted order as if it started there, taking positions modulo `n`, for the first id that is not below the target.

examples.note: The sorted order starts at position 2. The id 20 is at 3, 45 is met by 50 at 1, and 55 is above every id.
A ring not turned at all is plain sorted; 0 is below every id, so the smallest id at position 0 answers.

tests.call: (lambda r: (len(r), sum(r), r.count(-1)))(find_in_ring([2 * ((i + 61729) % 100000) for i in range(100000)], [(i * 7919) % 200003 for i in range(100000)]))

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Comparing with the last entry tells which side of the turn `mid` is on, even when there is no turn.
Comparing with the first entry fails on a ring that was never turned: every entry is at least the first.
One $O(\log n)$ search finds the turn and one more answers each lookup.

planted.slip: It searches for the first id above the target, so an id that is present is answered by the next one.
It finds the turn by comparing with the first entry, which puts the start at the end when the ring is not turned.
A dict answers ids that are present, but an absent id is walked up one at a time, which takes as many steps as the gap to the next id.
